title: Iraq begins high-stakes security balancing act as US troops withdraw
gist: With the last few hundred US troops leaving Iraq and Operation Inherent Resolve ending, PM Ali al-Zaidi is using the exit to politically delegitimise Iran-aligned militias ahead of a June 2027 disarmament deadline, but Iraq lacks air defence, key security ministers and regional calm. Experts warn of greater Iranian influence, possible US sanctions or strikes if militias keep targeting US assets, and stalled economic integration despite oil-led 'renaissance' pledges.

themes.theme: US exit as lever against Iran-aligned militias

insights.claim: The complete withdrawal of the remaining few hundred US troops from Iraq, ending the anti-ISIL coalition mission begun in 2015, is part of PM Ali al-Zaidi's strategy to 'politically weaken' militias, including Iran-linked ones, that cite the US presence to justify keeping their own weapons.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Removes the militias' main pretext for arms; watch whether disarmament actually progresses or militias openly refuse.
insights.quote: The prime minister is clearly trying to build a political case to Iraqis that these forces that are more beholden to Iran, and have used weapons without government authorisation, no longer have a political reason to have those weapons

insights.claim: Al-Zaidi pushed the deadline for bringing all weapons in Iraq under state control from September 30, 2026 to June 2027, and some militias have already indicated they will refuse to hand over their arms.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: June 2027 is the key date for a potential state-vs-militia confrontation that could disrupt Iraqi stability and oil output.
insights.locator: To be sure, al-Zaidi has already

insights.claim: According to al-Zaidi, both the US and Iran-aligned militias gave assurances to refrain from attacks for 90 days after the US withdrawal, a short-term firebreak rather than a durable settlement.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: The 90-day truce window expires around end-2026; escalation risk rises after it lapses.
insights.locator: Al-Zaidi told The New York Times

insights.claim: The withdrawal is a high-stakes gambit that leaves room for greater Iranian influence in Iraq and could lead to a catastrophic domestic standoff between the state and armed groups.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Iraq becomes a higher-variance geopolitical risk; monitor Iranian leverage over Baghdad politics.
insights.quote: It is a high-stakes gambit, leaving room for Iran to assert greater influence in the country and opening the door to a potentially catastrophic domestic standoff down the line.

themes.theme: Risk of Iraq becoming a US/Israeli target

insights.claim: Iran 'axis of resistance' militias in Iraq remain in 'full-on war mode' working with the IRGC and will keep targeting US interests, according to Chatham House's Renad Mansour.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Continued militia attacks keep US-Iraq relations fragile and raise tail risk for Iraqi territory being struck.
insights.quote: in full-on war mode, working with the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] in the region. And so they will continue to target US and US interests.

insights.claim: Baghdad's underlying anxiety is that the US may no longer need Iraq or may view it as a pariah state too close to Iran, which could bring sanctions or escalated US and Israeli strikes on Iraqi territory.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Sanctions on Iraq would hit a major oil exporter and its dollar access; a tail risk for oil and regional markets.
insights.quote: The anxiety from the Iraqi government now is that the US might not need Iraq any more, or might, in the worst case, view Iraq as a pariah state, too close to Iran, and therefore another target
insights.locator: The anxiety from the Iraqi government

insights.claim: Despite celebratory 'Sovereignty Days', parts of the Iraqi government are privately wary of the exit given ISIL sleeper cells, a shifting post-Assad Syria and the US-Israel war with Iran, fearing Iraq could be the next theatre of major regional conflict.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Official optimism understates security risk; discount public rhetoric when assessing Iraq stability.
insights.quote: But in reality, there is a great deal of concern that Iraq could be the next theatre of some major regional development

insights.claim: Iraq lacks a substantial air defence capability of its own, leaving it unable to defend against the drones, rockets and missiles pro-Iran militias have used against targets inside Iraq.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: A clear capability gap — potential demand for air-defence systems and a vulnerability if security spirals.
insights.quote: as of right now, the Iraqi military doesn’t really have a way to defend against that

insights.claim: The US military has reportedly removed its Erbil-based Patriot and C-RAM systems from Iraq, after they had this year thwarted a barrage of attacks on the Kurdish region by Iran and Iran-aligned militias; KRG PM Masrour Barzani called being left without defences 'shameful'.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Kurdish region (and its oil/energy infrastructure) is now more exposed to drone and missile attacks.
insights.quote: The threat is real – we are vulnerable, we are being attacked

insights.claim: Iraqi security forces, including the military, counterterrorism units and Popular Mobilisation Forces, have gained real capabilities against ISIL, which may limit operational fallout from the US exit, though key posts such as defence minister remain unfilled since a partial cabinet was approved in May.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Counter-ISIL resilience is decent, but governance gaps in the security ministries are a weak point to watch.
insights.locator: Several experts noted that Iraqi security

insights.claim: After the withdrawal the US and Iraq appear to be reverting to the 2008 Strategic Framework and Security Agreement, which pledges continued but non-binding US security support, with neither side clarifying future intelligence and logistics cooperation.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Ambiguous, non-binding commitments mean lower US deterrence in Iraq going forward.
insights.locator: In the wake of the withdrawal

insights.claim: A regional source expects the US-Iraq relationship to shift from a visible military footprint toward intelligence, training, technical support and capacity-building — a test of whether an intervention-era relationship can become a normal sovereign partnership.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Signals a lighter-touch US posture; defence-services and training contracts may replace troop presence.
insights.locator: However, a regional source with knowledge

insights.claim: International Crisis Group's Lahib Higel argues the US should preserve bilateral security cooperation rather than pressure al-Zaidi into a military confrontation with pro-Iran groups 'he is unlikely to win'.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: If Washington pushes confrontation anyway, risk of Iraqi internal conflict rises.
insights.quote: pressuring al-Zaidi into a military confrontation against pro-Iran groups that he is unlikely to win

insights.claim: Constriction of Strait of Hormuz traffic amid the US-Israel war with Iran cut Iraq's oil output by as much as 60 percent in March.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Shows Iraqi supply's acute exposure to Hormuz disruption — a key oil-supply sensitivity.

insights.claim: Al-Zaidi pledged an economic 'renaissance' including a bigger petrochemical industry and new fossil fuel export routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, while Trump promised 'a lot of deals' with Iraq citing its oil reserves.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Hormuz-bypass pipelines and US-Iraq energy deals are potential investment themes if security allows.

insights.claim: CNAS's Hamzeh Hadad says deeper US-Iraq economic integration may stall short term because regional conflict both hampers economic cooperation and gives armed groups an excuse to keep existing.
insights.speaker: Joseph Stepansky
insights.so_what: Don't expect quick US-Iraq commercial wins while the Iran war continues.
insights.quote: Conflict around Iraq will always make economic cooperation more difficult. Not to mention, conflict gives armed groups an excuse to continue to exist.
insights.locator: But deeper economic integration may be stalled
